KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...
A cold front is right on our doorstep to the west as of early this 
afternoon with showers and storms developing along and just ahead of 
the boundary, which are currently nearing the CT River. The 
environment this front will encounter across northern New 
England has effective shear of 40-50 kt over most of the area, 
per latest SPC mesoanalysis. In addition to this, around 500 
J/kg of SBCAPE is being analyzed across most of NH and far 
western ME and the western ME mountains for the next few hours,
which will be the primary areas to watch for a few strong to 
severe storms through early this evening due to the better 
instability/shear overlap, especially where more breaks in the 
clouds occur that could allow more localized CAPE upwards of 
1000 J/kg. Damaging winds, mainly from wet microbursts from the 
juicy airmass will be the primary hazard, but lowering freezing 
levels may also allow for hail to the size of quarters, although
lapse rates aloft aren't particularly favorable. Enough 
directional shear will also be present to support a brief 
tornado or two. 

Showers and storms could produce hefty rain rates but should be fast-
moving enough to where the risk of flash flooding is very low. The 
exceptions are around the Nashua/Manchester corridor and also across 
portions of Carroll and Oxford counties where earlier heavy rains 
fell, where a closer eye will need to be kept.

Once the front passes, chances for showers and storms will quickly 
diminish as the atmosphere quickly dries out. Based on latest CAM 
guidance, this should be by 6 to 7 pm for NH (although earlier 
for western NH) and then maybe an hour or so after that in far 
western ME. There will be probably be showers and a few storms 
continuing to advance along the front farther east into Maine 
this evening, but convection is expected to be on a weakening
trend as the environment will be less favorable.

Skies will continue to clear out from west to east this evening and 
overnight behind the front with mostly dry conditions other than a 
shower or two in the mountains. Patchy fog is possible where winds 
become light enough, but this should be mainly limited to river 
valleys. 

High pressure returns for Tuesday, bringing much quieter weather 
with plenty of sunshine. 850mb temps of +15C to +17C support highs 
reaching the mid to upper 80s south of the mountains with lower 
humidity as drier air aloft mixes down. Highs in and around the 
mountains will likely be a bit cooler and in the upper 70s to low 
80s. 

Mostly clear skies are expected Tuesday night with light winds, 
bringing a good opportunity for radiational cooling. Most of the 
area will see lows in the 50s, but some of the northern valleys 
could see lows in the mid-upper 40s. So I have gone a bit cooler 
than the NBM on lows. 


KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...Warming Trend Starts For the later 
half of the week

A warming trend will take hold starting Wed and last through 
the extended forecast. Sunny skies and mainly dry conditions 
will prevail as surface high pressure settles over the region 
and deep layer ridging builds overhead. H850 temps will rise 
from around 12C Tue up to 18°C Wed-Fri (potentially higher by 
Fri). Wednesday will be slightly warmer than Tue as the ridge 
axis shifts overhead, accompanied by increasing dewpoints. The 
warm advection accompanied by one or two weak waves could 
trigger a few scattered showers offshore that could clip the
coast, but not going to pin point it this far out. By Thursday 
and Friday, our region will become sandwiched between a Bermuda 
High shifting to our east and west, and a nearly stationary mid-
level trough over the Great Lakes. Broad and persistent sw flow
will drive dew points into the mid 60s to 70s by Friday. High 
temperatures will reach the 80s to near 90°F each afternoon, 
creating muggy conditions with heat index values reaching or 
exceeding 90°F in lower elevations. Nighttime temperatures will 
offer little relief, dropping only into the mid to upper 60s. 
The main chances for rain and thunderstorms will focus on 
Thursday through Friday, driven by a combination of a weakening 
cutoff low drifting northeast, a stalled or slow- moving frontal
boundary approaching from the west. Additional afternoon shower
activity may develop along local sea breezes, however warm air 
aloft (cap) will keep the activity spotty. While weak overall 
forcing should keep the severe weather threat low, any well 
timed diurnal shortwaves could be sufficient to trigger a few 
stronger thunderstorms. Any shower development during that 
period will have high rainfall rates,so locally heavy rainfall 
is possible. Overall the later half of the forecast will feature
mostly dry weather with plenty of sunshine and heat.
